checkpoints: Write functions with parameters and return values
Use lists, dictionaries, and loops comfortably
Understand what a virtual environment is and why it matters
Create a venv and install a package with pip

content.value: Flask is a Python framework, so you need to be comfortable with Python basics. Focus on functions (def), dictionaries (the data structure Flask uses everywhere for requests and responses), and loops. Virtual environments isolate your project's dependencies from your global Python installation — always use one. Run python -m venv venv, activate it with source venv/bin/activate (Mac/Linux) or venv\Scripts\activate (Windows), then pip install flask. The venv folder should be listed in .gitignore.

checkpoints: Install Flask and create app.py
Define a route with @app.route() and a view function
Return a string response from the view
Run the dev server with flask run

content.value: A Flask app is just a Python file. Import Flask, create an app instance, and decorate a function with @app.route('/') to map a URL to that function. The function returns what the client receives — start with a plain string, then move to JSON. Run flask run and visit http://127.0.0.1:5000 in your browser. Flask's built-in dev server reloads automatically when you save. The entire framework fits in your head — that's its superpower and the reason it's a great starting point for learning web backends.

checkpoints: Return JSON from a route using jsonify()
Accept GET and POST requests on the same route
Read JSON from a POST request body with request.get_json()
Understand HTTP status codes: 200, 201, 400, 404, 500

content.value: APIs communicate in JSON. Use Flask's jsonify() to return a dictionary as a proper JSON response with the correct Content-Type header. To accept both GET and POST on a route, add methods=['GET', 'POST'] to the decorator. In a POST handler, read the body with request.get_json(). Status codes signal success or failure: 200 OK, 201 Created (for new resources), 400 Bad Request (client sent invalid data), 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error. Always return the appropriate status code — clients use it to decide how to handle the response.

moduleTitle: Working with a Database using SQLite and Flask-SQLAlchemy
checkpoints: Install Flask-SQLAlchemy and configure a SQLite database
Define a model class that maps to a database table
Create the table by running db.create_all()
Insert, query, and delete records from the database
Understand what an ORM is and why it's useful

content.value: Databases store your app's data persistently. SQLite is a file-based database — perfect for development because there's nothing to install. Flask-SQLAlchemy is an ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) that lets you define database tables as Python classes and interact with them using Python instead of raw SQL. Define a model class that inherits from db.Model, add column definitions, and call db.create_all() inside an app context to create the table. Query with User.query.all() or User.query.filter_by(email=email).first(). Add, commit, and delete records through db.session.

checkpoints: Implement GET /items to return all records
Implement POST /items to create a new record
Implement GET /items/<id> to return one record
Implement PUT /items/<id> to update a record
Implement DELETE /items/<id> to delete a record
Test all endpoints with Postman or curl

content.value: CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) is the foundation of almost every API. Map the four operations to HTTP methods: POST creates, GET reads, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE deletes. Use URL parameters (<int:id>) to identify specific records. For each endpoint, validate the incoming data, perform the database operation, and return a meaningful response with the correct status code. Test with Postman — it lets you craft requests with any method, headers, and body without writing frontend code. Build a simple 'items' API and test every endpoint before moving on.

checkpoints: Use @app.errorhandler to return JSON error responses
Validate required fields in POST request bodies
Return 400 with a descriptive message for invalid input
Use abort() to trigger error responses from anywhere

content.value: A robust API never crashes silently. Use @app.errorhandler(404) and @app.errorhandler(500) to intercept errors and return structured JSON instead of HTML. Validate incoming data before touching the database — check that required fields exist, that strings aren't empty, and that numbers are within expected ranges. Return a 400 status code with a message like {'error': 'name is required'} when validation fails. The abort() function is a shortcut: abort(404) immediately triggers your 404 handler. Never trust client-provided data.

checkpoints: Build a complete CRUD API for to-do items
Each item has title, description, done (boolean), and created_at fields
Add a route to filter items by done status
Handle all validation and errors with proper status codes
Write a README documenting all endpoints

content.value: Your capstone is a complete, standalone API that a frontend could realistically consume. Build a to-do list API with full CRUD, a filter endpoint (/items?done=true), proper error handling, and a README that documents every endpoint with sample request and response bodies. Good documentation is a professional habit — it forces you to think about your API from the consumer's perspective. When the API is done, test every happy path and every error case with Postman and save the collection.
